newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya tenders for three power projects.
newsitem.headline: Kenya tenders for three power projects.

text.p: Kenya, which faces power shortages of up to 50 megawatts at peak hours, has placed international tenders for new projects to bridge the gap, a senior government energy official said on Thursday.
Crispus Mutitu, permanent secretary in the energy ministry, said Kenya would engage three or more companies to supplement the overworked national power grid, which has peak capacity of around 610 mw.
"The government had planned to engage only three companies but these may not be able to generate enough power to meet the national demand," Mutitu told Reuters in an interview.
"We expect to contract more than three companies which will be expected to generate between 30 and 50 megawatts as an addition to the national grid," the energy chief added.

Independent energy sources said the government had in fact narrowed the process, and was in direct negotiation with three companies on the tenders. The sources added that the tenders were for the provision of an extra 100 mw to 105 mw of power on a contract basis, higher than Mutitu's figures.
Because of the advanced technology involved, all the companies that will be accepted would be foreign, Mutitu said.
One of the projects would be a floating generator at the port of Mombasa.

Mutitu declined to say when Kenya placed the international tenders or give details of the deadline or whether the government had already made known any preferences. In Nairobi business circles, it is known that there has been intense lobbying from French, British, German, Japanese and Singaporean companies.
The tenders are expected to be opened this month and contracts that follow should see power available by mid-1997, senior government energy sources said.
Mutitu did not say how much money was involved. He would also not say whether the entire project was funded by the government or Western donor countries and institutions.
Mutitu said some of the companies would be contracted to replace existing power generation equipment which is old and partly responsible for the chronic shortages.

Manufacturing companies in Kenya complain of problems caused by peak evening demand which is 15 mw in excess of maximum generating and transmission capacity. The deficit can rise to 50 mw or more because of breakdowns and essential maintenance.

The Kenya Power & Lighting Company (KP&LC) said negotiations on financing its 1.2-billion-shilling ($21 million) medium-term power development programme continue slowly and the World Bank is reasonably optimistic funding may be agreed by the end of 1996.

But even the first project, a 75 mw thermal generating station for which funding had been agreed with the government of Japan, is unlikely to feed power into the grid before 1999. ($1=56.92 shillings) -- Nairobi Newsroom ++254-2 330-261
